Title: How Your Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills: An Empirical Study
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that operate within privileged execution environments and routinely handle sensitive credentials, yet how these credentials are leaked remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first large-scale empirical study on credential leakage in agent skills. From 170,226 artifacts on SkillsMP, the largest open-source skill marketplace, we sampled 17,022 skills via stratified random sampling and analyzed each through static secret extraction (regex and AST parsing), dynamic sandbox testing of flagged candidates seeded with mock credentials, and cross-referencing developer intent against runtime behavior. Our analysis identifies 520 affected skills containing 1,708 security issues, and yields a taxonomy of 10 leakage patterns. Three findings stand out. First, 76.3% of cases require jointly analyzing natural-language descriptions and programming logic, showing that credential exposure in skills is fundamentally cross-modal. Second, Information Exposure accounts for 73.5% of vulnerability issues because agent frameworks feed stdout into the LLM context window, turning routine debugging into a credential exposure vector. Third, 89.6% of leaked credentials are immediately exploitable, and the fork-based distribution model defeats remediation, as secrets removed from upstream repositories persist across 50+ independent forks. Following responsible disclosure, all malicious skills have been removed. We release our dataset, taxonomy, and detection pipeline to support future agent security research.
Major_Contribution_Result: The paper reports a large-scale empirical study of credential leakage in LLM agent skills. From 170,226 SkillsMP artifacts, the authors sampled 17,022 skills and identified 1,708 security issues across 520 affected skills (3.1%), plus a taxonomy of 10 leakage patterns. They report that 76.3% of cases require jointly analyzing natural-language descriptions and executable code; developer negligence accounts for 84.0% of cases; debug logging via print/console.log alone accounts for 73.5% of vulnerability patterns; and dynamic testing finds 89.6% of affected skills exploitable during routine execution without elevated privileges. Responsible disclosure led to removal of 83 malicious skills and remediation of 91.6% of identified hardcoded-credential cases.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: In Threats to Validity, the authors note that classifying accidental versus deliberate leakage is subjective (three experts; mean Cohen's κ=0.88) and the taxonomy may miss unanticipated patterns. AST-based credential-flow analysis covers only Python and JavaScript at the intra-procedural level; other languages fall back to keyword matching, and cross-variable propagation is not tracked. Dynamic sandboxing can miss dormant or non-deterministic paths. Externally, all data come from SkillsMP, so prevalence on other platforms may differ.
Critics: This contribution is a supply-chain measurement and taxonomy of credential exposure in agent skills, not a comparative evaluation of agent runtime defenses against prompt injection or tool hijacking. Strengths for SLR use include concrete sampled counts, a leakage taxonomy, and disclosure outcomes; limits include single-marketplace sampling and incomplete static analysis coverage. It informs agent-security evaluation at the skill/package trust boundary but does not define a full agent attack–defense–reassessment lifecycle.
